messages.author: 7e3dd9d1a219437c
messages.subject: Distance survey design
parts:
Hi everyone,

I am working on my thesis proposal and I am strugling with some things. I would like to look at the effect of framentation on the population size of the blue-eyed black lemur in Madagascar. I also want to make an estimate the population size in these fragments and an estimation on the total population size. Hereby, I would like to make use of line-transect with the distance sampling method. Because the vegatation can be very dense, and the chance of detecting an animal can fast decrease with an increase in distance from the observer. However, a detailed map of the area is not available, and we are not sure if we are able to make a detailed map out of satalite photes (with information of 2014, so already quit some years ago..). These satalite images showed that the fragments are really small and very long stretched.

So if I follow the Buckland (2001) literature a minimum between 60-80 observation is required to reliaby estimate detection probability. Or even larger to yield a good precision fort he estimation of abundance. I also found that 10-20 lines is required, preferably closer to 20.

These “requirements” may not possible for us as the fragments may be to small. However, to answer my research questions it is important to look in different forest fragment with different sizes. I have think of many possible solutions, but I am stuck on the moment.

 

My questions to you are:

-       - How would you make this survey design?

-       - Or do I have to drop the size of fragment, and maybe look at a larger survey area which includ different forest fragments and conduct line transect surveys in this total area. So you than may cross different habitat types or forest fragments

-        -  If it is possible to do line transect surveys, how could I deal with al these small and stretched fragments. How could I determine where the line should be. (along with the stretch, or perpendicular on the fragment?

-       -   Or do I have to use other methods than distance sampling? :P

 

Thank you in advance!

Jessica

messages.author: f2122b34f1aa6e95
messages.subject: Re: [distance-sampling] Distance survey design
parts:
Jessica

These are good questions to ask at the design stage of your study.  Placing survey effort within fragmented habitat is difficult and accumulating the desired number of detections (particularly of a species presumably so rare (Volampeno et al. 2011 http://www.karger.com/Article/Abstract/322231)).

I cannot precisely answer your question about creating a design for such a survey lacking precise information about the size of the fragments.  You might have a look at this paper dealing with a small population of animals of similar body size to your lemurs for ideas about their design.  Note their species was vocal, so they were able to use aural cues:

Savage, Anne, Len Thomas, Katherine A. Leighty, Luis H. Soto, and Felix S. Medina. 2010. ‘Novel Survey Method Finds Dramatic Decline of Wild Cotton-Top Tamarin Population’. Nature Communications 1 (June): 30. https://www.nature.com/articles/ncomms1030


Perhaps the size of your fragments might make the use of point transects more useful.  See this example (for birds) of a survey design for a 32ha forest

Buckland, Stephen T. ‘Point-transect surveys for songbirds: robust methodologies’. The Auk 123 (2): 345–57. doi:10.1642/0004-8038(2006)123[345:PSFSRM]2.0.CO;2.

Possibly detections of animals will be too few to reliably estimate density; however if you can detect the faeces they leave behind, you might be able to estimate dung density and convert that (by estimating deposition and decay rates) into lemur density as was done in this study of forest fragments in Scotland

Marques, Fernanda F.C., Stephen T. Buckland, David Goffin, Camilla E. Dixon, David L. Borchers, Brenda A. Mayle, and Andrew J. Peace. 2001. ‘Estimating Deer Abundance from Line Transect Surveys of Dung: Sika Deer in Southern Scotland’. Journal of Applied Ecology 38 (2): 349–63. doi:10.1046/j.1365-2664.2001.00584.x.


Lastly, the recommended number of transects is needed if inference regarding abundance is design-based.  An alternative form of inference is "model-based" and might be applicable in your situation (which requires modelling of not only the detection function but also modelling the encounter rate perhaps using environmental covariates); see

Miller, David L., M. Louise Burt, Eric A. Rexstad, and Len Thomas. 2013. ‘Spatial Models for Distance Sampling Data: Recent Developments and Future Directions’. Methods in Ecology and Evolution 4 (11): 1001–10. doi:10.1111/2041-210X.12105.

Those are some suggestions that may prove useful.
